title: Life as a banquet
hook: when a dish reaches you, take a modest share; if it passes, don't reach after it (Enchiridion 15)

segments.voice: Yesterday: who holds the leash. That was also your line. When something tugged you, did you loosen your end a little? Day three hundred forty-seven.

A big family dinner. The bowls go around the table, left to right. Mashed potatoes, the good rolls, the one dish everyone fights over. You can see it coming, four people away. There's an uncle who has already half stood up to reach for it. There's a cousin watching it with her fork raised. And there's one person, usually an older aunt, who just talks to whoever's beside her, takes a spoonful when the bowl arrives, and passes it on. Epictetus would have liked that aunt. Section fifteen of the handbook is set at exactly this kind of table. Today: life as a banquet.
screen: `BOWLS GOING AROUND THE TABLE.` → `THE UNCLE HALF STANDING.` → `THE AUNT WHO JUST PASSES IT ON.`

segments.voice: First, the table. Remember, Epictetus says, to behave in life as at a banquet. A dish is carried around and reaches you: put out your hand and take a modest share. Second, the two moments of restraint. It passes you by: don't hold it back. It hasn't come yet: don't send your desire out ahead to meet it. Wait until it's in front of you. That second one is subtle. A lot of our grabbing happens before anything arrives, in our heads, at the promotion we haven't been offered, the house we haven't seen, the relationship we're already planning. Third, what's on the dishes. Do the same, he says, with children, with a spouse, with office, with wealth. They come around. They pass. Take your share well when they reach you. And then, he says, you'll be a worthy guest at the banquet of the gods. He adds a further step, for a few: if you can let some dishes go by even when they're offered, you'll share not just the gods' table but their rule. He names Diogenes the Cynic and Heraclitus as people who lived that way. Fourth, the word. Banquet here is symposion, a drinking together, the same word as Plato's dialogue. Ancient dinners had customs about how the dishes and the cup moved. Epictetus is borrowing manners everyone knew and turning them into a whole philosophy of having. Good things come around. Take a fair share. Pass it on. Don't lean down the table after the next bowl.
screen: `A DISH REACHES YOU: A MODEST SHARE.` · `PASSED: DON'T HOLD IT. NOT YET: WAIT.` · `CHILDREN, OFFICE, WEALTH, ON THE DISHES.` · `SYMPOSION: DRINKING TOGETHER.` · then, large: `WHEN THE DISH COMES.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're reaching ahead for. Something that hasn't come to your end of the table yet: a trip, a result, a bit of good news. Notice your hand, as it were, already stretched toward it. Gently bring the hand back to your lap. Say inside: when the dish comes. Then look at what's in front of you right now, this breath, this chair, this moment, and take a modest share of it. The bell holds the time.
Life as a banquet. Epictetus' table manners for living: take a modest share when the dish reaches you, let it pass, and don't reach ahead. Today's word.
Your line: when the dish comes. Take a modest share of one thing today, food, praise, time, and pass the rest along. Day three hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners treat good things as dishes passed at a banquet: they take a moderate share when one arrives, and try not to grasp ahead or hold on as it passes.

options: reach down the table for it.
wait until it's in front of you.
ask everyone to skip their turn.
fork.reveal: don't send your desire ahead, he says. wait until it reaches you, then take a modest share.

original.note: Greek, Enchiridion 15: a banquet, literally a drinking together.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be greedy at dinner.
what it means: good things come around and pass; take a modest share, don't grab ahead, don't hold on.
what a scholar hears: symposion, the same word as Plato's dialogue; the 'banquet of the gods' line ends with Diogenes and Heraclitus as models.

notes: Enchiridion 15 paraphrased (dish carried round; moderate portion; passes by; not yet come; children, wife, magisterial offices, wealth; worthy partner of the gods' banquets; share their rule; Diogenes and Heraclitus). Confirm.
Greek συμπόσιον in Enchiridion 15 ('ὡς ἐν συμποσίῳ'): confirm.
The family-dinner scene is an illustration.
